title: Exploring Data with Summary Statistics 📈
description: Use mean, median, mode, variance, and correlation to peek inside your data.

slides.title: Get to Know Your Data 🔍
slides.content:
# Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Before building a model, you must **understand your data**.

EDA involves:
- Summary statistics (mean, median, spread).
- Visualisations (histograms, scatter plots).
- Spotting anomalies, patterns, relationships.

Think of it like a doctor checking a patient’s vitals before prescribing medicine.

slides.title: Measures of Central Tendency 🎯
slides.content:
# Mean, Median, Mode

- **Mean**: average (sum of values / count). Sensitive to outliers.
- **Median**: the middle value when sorted. Robust to outliers.
- **Mode**: the most frequent value. Useful for categorical data.

*Example*: incomes [30k, 35k, 40k, 45k, 500k] — mean = 130k (skewed), median = 40k (better represents typical).

quizData.question: Why might the median be preferred over the mean for house prices?

options.text: Median is always easier to compute
Median is not affected by extremely expensive mansions
Median gives a more exciting number

quizData.explanation: A few luxury homes can pull the mean upward; the median stays representative of the typical house.

slides.title: Measures of Spread 📏
slides.content:
# Variance, Standard Deviation, IQR

- **Variance**: average squared deviation from the mean. Hard to interpret directly.
- **Standard Deviation (std)**: square root of variance; same unit as data. Tells how spread out values are.
- **Percentiles & IQR**: the 25th, 50th, 75th percentiles. IQR = Q3 – Q1, robust to outliers.

These help you spot distributions that are wide (diverse) or narrow (clustered).

slides.title: EDA in Python 🐍
slides.codeSnippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({'age': [22, 35, 58, 41, 29, 33]})
print(df.describe())

slides.title: Correlation: Are Features Linked? 🔗
slides.content:
# Relationships Between Variables

- **Correlation coefficient (r)** measures linear relationship between two numerical features. Range: -1 to +1.
  - +1: perfect positive (as X increases, Y increases).
  - -1: perfect negative.
  - 0: no linear relation.

- High correlation between features can cause problems (multicollinearity) in some models.

- Correlation ≠ causation! Ice cream sales and drowning rates correlate (both increase in summer), but one doesn’t cause the other.

quizData.question: If two variables have a correlation of -0.9, they have a strong negative linear relationship.
quizData.explanation: True. -0.9 indicates a strong inverse relationship: as one goes up, the other goes down.
